title: Quicksort
oneLiner: Partition around a pivot, then quicksort each side. O(n log n) on average, in place, and the usual fastest general sort in practice.
keyTakeaway: Quicksort puts one pivot in its final place with an O(n) partition, then recurses on the two sides. Good pivots halve the range, giving O(n log n); a pivot that is always the smallest or largest gives O(n²). Picking the middle element (or a random one) makes that worst case unlikely on real data.
explanation:
Return nums sorted in ascending order using quicksort. The partition step from Quicksort Partition, earlier in this track, does the real work: it rearranges a range so everything smaller than the pivot comes first, then the pivot, then everything else, and tells you where the pivot landed. That pivot is now in its final sorted position.

Quicksort just repeats that. Sort(lo, hi): if the range has fewer than 2 elements, stop. Otherwise partition it, getting the pivot's index p, then Sort(lo, p - 1) and Sort(p + 1, hi). Nothing needs combining afterwards: once both sides are sorted, the whole range is sorted, because every element on the left is smaller than the pivot and every element on the right is not.

Use the Lomuto partition you already know, with the last element of the range as the pivot. Before partitioning, swap the middle element of the range into the last slot. On already sorted input, always using the last element as pivot would split n into n - 1 and 0 at every level: n levels of O(n) work, O(n²). Taking the middle element splits sorted input evenly.

On average quicksort is O(n log n) with about log n levels of recursion, and it sorts in place, needing only the O(log n) recursion stack. Its inner loop is a tight compare and swap over contiguous memory, which is why it usually beats merge sort in practice. It is not stable. Real libraries (C#'s Array.Sort uses introsort) switch to heap sort if the recursion gets too deep, which caps the worst case at O(n log n).

The visualization sorts [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] and highlights each pivot once it is in its final place.

recognitionSignals: Sort in place with O(log n) extra space and good average speed.
Any problem built on partition: k-th smallest or largest (quickselect), Dutch national flag, moving values that match a test to one side.
gotchas: Always taking the first or last element as pivot makes sorted or reversed input O(n²) with n levels of recursion.
Recursing on (lo, p) instead of (lo, p - 1) includes the pivot again and can loop forever when p == hi.
Lomuto partition with many equal values still works but degrades; three-way partitioning (see Sort Colors) handles duplicates best.
confusableWith: Merge sort does its work after the recursive calls (merging) and is stable but needs O(n) space; quicksort does its work before (partitioning), in place, and is not stable.
Quickselect partitions the same way but recurses into only the side that holds the k-th element, so it averages O(n) instead of O(n log n).

complexity.note: On average each partition splits the range roughly in half: about log n levels, O(n) partition work per level. The worst case, when pivots are always the extremes, is O(n²) with O(n) recursion depth; the middle pivot avoids that on sorted input. Sorting is in place, so the extra space is the recursion stack. (This version copies the input first, which is another O(n).)

referenceSolutions.python:
def quick_sort(nums):
    a = list(nums)

    def sort(lo, hi):
        if lo >= hi:
            return
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        a[mid], a[hi] = a[hi], a[mid]  # middle pivot: sorted input still splits evenly
        pivot = a[hi]
        i = lo
        for j in range(lo, hi):
            if a[j] < pivot:
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
                i += 1
        a[i], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i]
        sort(lo, i - 1)
        sort(i + 1, hi)

    sort(0, len(a) - 1)
    return a
